power-duration-curve.short: The best power (or speed) a person can hold, plotted against how long they can hold it. Steep for short efforts, then levelling off towards critical power.

hyperbola.short: A curve that falls steeply, then flattens and creeps ever closer to a line without reaching it. Best power against time, between about 2 and 15 min, has this shape.

asymptote.short: A line that a curve gets closer and closer to but never reaches. Critical power is the asymptote of the power–duration curve.

w-prime.short: The fixed amount of work, in kJ, that you can do above critical power before you must slow down. Hard efforts above CP use it up; riding below CP slowly refills it.

severe-domain.short: Efforts above critical power. Oxygen uptake climbs to its maximum and lactate keeps rising, so the effort ends within minutes: the harder, the sooner.

vo2-slow-component.short: A slow extra rise in oxygen uptake during hard constant-power exercise, after the first quick rise. Above critical power it carries oxygen uptake up to its maximum.

time-to-exhaustion.short: How long a person can keep up a set power or speed before they can't go on. Several of them, at different powers, map out the power–duration curve.

linear-regression.short: A method that fits the best straight line through a set of points. It gives the line's slope (rise per unit of x) and intercept (where it crosses the y-axis).

three-minute-all-out-test.short: A 3-minute effort flat out from the first second, with no pacing. Power falls, then levels off; the power over the last 30 s is used to estimate critical power.

w-prime-balance.short: How much of W′ is left at a given moment: it falls whenever power is above critical power and slowly refills when power is below it.

criterium.short: A short road race on a small closed circuit of many laps. Tight corners make riders sprint out of each one, so power swings up and down all race.

maximal-metabolic-steady-state.short: The highest intensity at which oxygen uptake, blood lactate and muscle chemistry can still level off. Critical power and MLSS are two ways to estimate it.

limits-of-agreement.short: The range that holds 95% of the differences between two methods used on the same people. Wide limits mean one can't stand in for the other in a single person, even if the averages match.

critical-speed.short: The running (or swimming) form of critical power, in m·s⁻¹: the speed the speed–duration curve levels off at. Below it, running can settle into a steady state.

d-prime.short: D′ ('D prime'): a fixed distance, in metres, that a runner can cover above critical speed. The running form of W′.

riegel-formula.short: A rule that predicts a longer race time from a shorter one: T₂ = T₁ × (D₂ ÷ D₁)^1.06. The exponent sets how much a runner slows as the distance grows.
